summary: Proposes a Telnet option that lets the serving host control when characters typed by a user are echoed and when they are sent. The aim is to cut down the number of network messages that character-at-a-time typing with remote echo would otherwise need.

eli5.summary: Typing on a faraway computer sends a message for every letter. This idea lets the far computer say to bundle the letters, so fewer messages are needed.

questions: what is the rcte telnet option
how to reduce telnet echo traffic
what is a break character in telnet rcte
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets the server tell the user's host when to echo typing and when to send it.

tldr.problem: With character-at-a-time typing and foreign-host echo, each character struck costs four network messages: the character, its RFNM, the echo and its RFNM.
tldr.mechanism: The Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing option (RCTE) has the user host hold echoes and buffer typing, while the server sends small commands saying what to echo and which characters trigger a send.
tldr.outcome: The authors believe almost a 90 per cent reduction in character-mode interactive terminal traffic is attainable. It is updated by RFC 581.

today: RFC 560 was updated by RFC 581. The RFC index lists its status as Unknown, and the text does not say whether the option was deployed.

sections.title: The Cost of Echoing
sections.content:
With a terminal in character-at-a-time mode and the foreign host doing the echo, every character struck causes four network messages. Eliminating most echoing halves the count, and packaging characters into units of about five cuts it by another 80 per cent. The authors believe this gives almost a 90 per cent reduction and should also lighten the load on foreign hosts.

The text also cites the echo delay seen by users reaching a full-duplex host over a satellite link, and proposes an echo control like those of some time-sharing systems. The option is meant only for full-duplex hosts. The Go-Ahead feature is adequate for half-duplex servers.
sections.eli5: Sending every letter one at a time and getting each one echoed back is slow and wasteful. Bundling letters is much cheaper.

sections.title: Turning the Option On
sections.content:
The option is called RCTE and uses the usual Telnet commands. IAC WILL RCTE says the sender will send instructions for controlling the other side's terminal printer, and IAC DO RCTE agrees to be controlled. WON'T and DON'T refuse. The default is WON'T RCTE and DON'T RCTE, so neither host controls the other's printer.

Once agreed, the using host only acts on the controlling (serving) host's commands. It sends no RCTE commands unless it decides to stop the option with IAC DON'T RCTE.
sections.eli5: First the two computers agree that the far one is allowed to boss the near one's screen. If they do not agree, nothing changes.

sections.title: The RCTE Command Byte
sections.content:
The server controls the user host with IAC SB RCTE <cmd> [BC1 BC2] [TC1 TC2]. Bit 0 of <cmd> set to 0 means repeat the last command. Bit 1 says whether to echo the Break character, bit 2 whether to echo the text up to it, bit 3 that two bytes of new Break classes follow, and bit 4 that two bytes of new Transmit classes follow.

A Transmission character requires the user host to send all text collected so far, and hosts are discouraged from sending earlier. A Break character does the same and also ends the current print or discard action until the next command. Nine character classes are defined, such as letters, numbers, format effectors, punctuation and space. At start-up no Transmission classes are in effect, and classes 4, 5 and 9 are Break classes. Telnet commands always act as Break characters.

Even-numbered values above zero are errors and are treated as zero.
sections.eli5: The far computer sends a tiny coded note: show what I type, hide it, or hide just the last key, and send my words when I press certain keys such as space or return.

sections.title: How a Session Works
sections.content:
The user host starts by holding back echo printing until a command arrives. Server output is printed immediately, and text from the server MUST end with an RCTE command. Typed input is buffered up to a Transmission or Break character and echoed or not as the latest command says. A Break character completes the cycle, and any server output restarts it.

A sample logon to a TENEX system shows a password not being echoed, because the server instructs the user host to skip it. The notes warn that large overhead makes RCTE unjustified for true character-at-a-time use, and that type-ahead buffering, especially on TIPs, may overflow.

Per the RFC, these sub-commands are only sent by the controlling host and functionally replace the Go-Ahead command.
sections.eli5: Your computer waits, collects what you type, and shows or hides it as the far computer says. It sends your words in chunks. A password is hidden this way.

items.label: Continue
items.desc: Continue what you have been doing.

items.label: Print all
items.desc: Print up to and including the Break character.

items.label: Skip Break
items.desc: Print up to the Break character but do not echo it.

items.label: Skip text
items.desc: Do not echo text, but print the Break character.

items.label: Skip all
items.desc: Skip up to and including the Break character.

items.label: Set Break classes
items.desc: Add to a value above; BC1 BC2 follow.

items.label: Set Transmit classes
items.desc: Add to a value above; TC1 TC2 follow.

items.label: Set both
items.desc: Break classes first, then Transmit classes.
